shots.phrase: Begin by framing Course Foundations and Scope as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.
In this course, students will explore puzzle solving and creation as a way of exploring human-inspired algorithm development and the synergy of humans and computers to develop programmatic solutions.
List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion.
Now define Logical Puzzles and Constraint Satisfaction precisely enough that another learner could test the definition.
Consider this worked case: A Sudoku solver uses backtracking to assign digits 1-9 to empty cells while maintaining row, column, and box constraints.
, a red circle around a row) and a step-by-step animation of a cell being filled based on eliminated options.
With the foundation in place, examine how Maze Algorithms and Graph Traversal operates in a concrete sequence.
Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions.
Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition.
Next, compare the choices involved in Optimization Puzzles and Heuristics and make the decision criteria explicit.
For each type of puzzle, students will develop and implement both optimal solving algorithms and algorithms that mimic human solving processes.
Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts.
Apply Word Puzzles and String Processing to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition.
Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits.
Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step.
Examine the tradeoffs in Algorithmic Paradigms and Data Structures, including what improves and what becomes more difficult.
Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms.
State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable.
Stress-test the reasoning around Human-Inspired vs.
Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms.
Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds.
Use Puzzle Generation and Human Solvability to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action.
Finally, they will discuss and solve puzzle hunts, which include puzzles without any instruction and apparent ambiguity, yet are still uniquely solvable for humans.
Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause.
Connect Puzzle Hunts and Ambiguity Resolution to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system.
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises.
Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations.
Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis.
They will also write programs that construct certain types of puzzles with human solvers in mind.
For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step.
